EKG Reading Notes: A Comprehensive Reference 
Table of Contents 
1.   Foundations 
2.   Waveform Components 
3.   A Systematic Approach 
4.   Rate 
5.   Rhythm Analysis 
6.   Axis Determination 
7.   Intervals and Segments 
8.   Conduction Abnormalities 
9.   Chamber Enlargement and Hypertrophy 
10.   Ischemia and Infarction 
11.   Electrolyte Abnormalities 
12.   Important "Can't-Miss" Patterns 
13.   Pacemakers 
14.   Artifact vs. Pathology 
15.   Quick Reference Summary 
1. Foundations 
What an EKG Measures 
An electrocardiogram records the electrical activity of the heart from the body's surface. Each
lead views the heart from a di ff erent angle, producing a unique tracing. The size and direction of
each de fl ection re fl ect the net vector of electrical depolarization or repolarization relative to that
lead's axis. 
The 12-Lead System 
Limb leads (frontal plane): 
Bipolar leads:   I, II, III 
Augmented leads:   aVR, aVL, aVF 
Precordial leads (horizontal plane):   V1 through V6

Lead groupings by anatomy: 
Region   Leads   Artery (usually) 
Inferior   II, III, aVF   RCA (80%) or LCx 
Lateral   I, aVL, V5, V6   LCx or diagonal 
Anterior   V3, V4   LAD 
Septal   V1, V2   LAD (proximal) 
High lateral   I, aVL   LCx 
Posterior   Mirror in V1–V3   RCA or LCx 
Paper Speed and Calibration 
Standard speed:   25 mm/second 
Standard calibration:   10 mm = 1 mV 
Small box:   1 mm wide (0.04 sec), 1 mm tall (0.1 mV) 
Large box:   5 mm wide (0.20 sec), 5 mm tall (0.5 mV) 
Always con fi rm the calibration square wave before interpreting — half-standard or double-
standard tracings will mislead you. 
2. Waveform Components 
P Wave 
Represents atrial depolarization. 
Normal duration:   < 0.12 sec (< 3 small boxes) 
Normal amplitude:   < 2.5 mm 
Best seen in:   Lead II (for rhythm) and V1 (for morphology) 
Upright in I, II, aVF; inverted in aVR (in sinus rhythm) 
PR Interval 
From start of P to start of QRS — atrial depolarization plus AV node delay. 
Normal:   0.12–0.20 sec (3–5 small boxes)

Short → pre-excitation (e.g., WPW) 
Long →   fi rst-degree AV block 
QRS Complex 
Ventricular depolarization. 
Normal duration:   < 0.12 sec (< 3 small boxes); narrow complexes are supraventricular in
origin, wide complexes suggest ventricular origin or aberrant conduction. 
Q wave:   fi rst negative de fl ection 
R wave:   fi rst positive de fl ection 
S wave:   negative de fl ection following R 
ST Segment 
End of QRS (J point) to start of T wave. Should be isoelectric. Elevation or depression can
indicate ischemia, injury, pericarditis, early repolarization, or LV strain. 
T Wave 
Ventricular repolarization. 
Usually upright in I, II, V3–V6 
Inverted in aVR 
Variable in III, aVL, V1–V2 
Tall, peaked T waves → hyperkalemia or hyperacute ischemia 
Inverted T waves → ischemia, strain, CNS events 
QT Interval 
From start of QRS to end of T. Re fl ects total ventricular depolarization plus repolarization. Must
be   corrected for rate (QTc)   using Bazett's formula: QTc = QT /   √ RR. 
Normal QTc:   < 440 ms (men), < 460 ms (women) 
Prolonged QTc > 500 ms:   signi fi cant risk of torsades de pointes 
U Wave 
Small de fl ection after T. Prominent U waves suggest hypokalemia, bradycardia, or drug e ff ect. 
3. A Systematic Approach to Reading Every EKG

Never interpret piecemeal. Use the same sequence every time so nothing gets missed: 
1.   Con fi rm patient data and calibration   (name, date, standard or half-standard) 
2.   Rate 
3.   Rhythm 
4.   Axis 
5.   Intervals   (PR, QRS, QT/QTc) 
6.   P wave morphology 
7.   QRS morphology   (voltage, Q waves, R-wave progression) 
8.   ST segment   (elevation, depression, J-point) 
9.   T waves   (direction, symmetry, amplitude) 
10.   Overall clinical impression   — always synthesize   fi ndings with the patient in front of you 
4. Rate 
Methods 
300 method:   Count large boxes between two R waves; divide 300 by that number.
Memorize: 300, 150, 100, 75, 60, 50, 43, 37. 
1500 method:   Count small boxes between R waves; divide 1500 by that number. Most
precise for regular rhythms. 
6-second method:   Count QRS complexes in 30 large boxes (6 sec) and multiply by 10. Best
for irregular rhythms. 
De fi nitions 
Bradycardia:   < 60 bpm 
Normal:   60–100 bpm 
Tachycardia:   > 100 bpm 
5. Rhythm Analysis 
Criteria for Normal Sinus Rhythm 
Rate 60–100 bpm 
Regular R-R intervals

P before every QRS, QRS after every P 
P waves upright in I, II, aVF; inverted in aVR 
Constant PR interval (0.12–0.20 sec) 
Sinus Variants 
Sinus bradycardia:   NSR with rate < 60 
Sinus tachycardia:   NSR with rate > 100 
Sinus arrhythmia:   phasic variation with respiration (common and benign in young
patients) 
Atrial Arrhythmias 
Premature Atrial Contraction (PAC):   Early P wave with abnormal morphology, usually followed
by a narrow QRS. 
Atrial Fibrillation: 
Irregularly irregular rhythm 
No discernible P waves — chaotic   fi brillatory baseline 
Variable ventricular response 
Atrial Flutter: 
"Sawtooth"   fl utter waves, typically at ~300 bpm atrial rate 
Commonly conducts 2:1 (ventricular rate ~150 bpm) 
Regular unless variable block present 
Multifocal Atrial Tachycardia (MAT): 
Rate > 100 
At least 3 distinct P-wave morphologies 
Often in COPD patients 
Supraventricular Tachycardia (SVT): 
Narrow complex, regular, rate typically 150–250 
P waves often buried in QRS or appear as retrograde pseudo-R' in V1

Junctional Rhythms 
Narrow QRS, rate 40–60 (junctional escape) or 60–100 (accelerated) 
Inverted or absent P waves, or P buried in QRS 
Ventricular   Arrhythmias 
Premature Ventricular Contraction (PVC):   Wide, bizarre QRS without preceding P; typically
followed by a compensatory pause. 
Ventricular Tachycardia (VT): 
≥ 3 consecutive PVCs at rate > 100 
Wide QRS (> 0.12 sec) 
Monomorphic or polymorphic 
Sustained   if > 30 seconds or hemodynamically unstable 
Treat any wide-complex tachycardia as VT until proven otherwise 
Torsades de Pointes:   Polymorphic VT with QRS amplitude that twists around the baseline;
arises in the setting of prolonged QT. 
Ventricular Fibrillation:   Chaotic, irregular de fl ections without identi fi able QRS complexes.
Immediately fatal without de fi brillation. 
Asystole:   Flat line (con fi rm in more than one lead to exclude lead disconnection). 
Idioventricular rhythm:   Wide QRS, rate 20–40, no P waves. "Accelerated" idioventricular
rhythm runs 40–120 and is a classic reperfusion rhythm post-MI. 
6. Axis Determination 
The "axis" refers to the net direction of ventricular depolarization in the frontal plane. 
Quick Method — The Two-Lead Shortcut 
Lead I   Lead aVF   Axis 
Positive   Positive   Normal (-30° to +90°) 
Positive   Negative   Possible Left Axis Deviation (check II) 
Negative   Positive   Right Axis Deviation

Lead I   Lead aVF   Axis 
Negative   Negative   Extreme axis ("Northwest") 
If Lead I is positive and aVF is negative, look at Lead II: if II is also positive, the axis is still normal;
if II is negative, it's LAD. 
Common Causes 
Left axis deviation:   LVH, left anterior fascicular block, inferior MI, WPW 
Right axis deviation:   RVH, left posterior fascicular block, lateral MI, PE, pediatric normal 
Extreme axis:   Ventricular rhythm, severe RVH, hyperkalemia 
7. Intervals and Segments 
PR Interval 
Short (< 120 ms):   WPW, LGL, junctional rhythm 
Long (> 200 ms):   First-degree AV block 
QRS Duration 
Narrow (< 120 ms):   Supraventricular origin 
Wide (≥ 120 ms):   Bundle branch block, ventricular rhythm, hyperkalemia, sodium channel
blocker toxicity, pre-excitation 
QT / QTc 
Measure in lead II or V5, ideally where T waves are most distinct 
QTc > 500 ms raises torsades risk signi fi cantly 
Common causes of prolonged QT: congenital long QT syndromes, hypokalemia,
hypomagnesemia, hypocalcemia, antiarrhythmics (sotalol, amiodarone), antipsychotics,
macrolides,   fl uoroquinolones, methadone

8. Conduction Abnormalities 
AV Blocks 
First-degree AV block: 
PR > 200 ms, constant 
Every P conducts; benign in isolation 
Second-degree AV block, Mobitz I (Wenckebach): 
Progressive PR prolongation until a P fails to conduct 
R-R interval shortens before the dropped beat 
Usually   AV nodal, often benign, rarely requires pacing 
Second-degree AV block, Mobitz II: 
Fixed PR interval with intermittent dropped QRS 
Typically infranodal (His-Purkinje) 
High risk of progression to complete block; usually requires pacing 
Third-degree (complete) AV block: 
Complete AV dissociation 
Atrial and ventricular rates independent 
Escape rhythm determines QRS width: narrow (junctional escape) or wide (ventricular
escape) 
Requires pacing 
Bundle Branch Blocks 
Right Bundle Branch Block (RBBB): 
QRS ≥ 120 ms 
rSR' ("bunny ears") in V1 
Wide slurred S wave in I, V6 
Normal axis usually preserved 
Left Bundle Branch Block (LBBB): 
QRS ≥ 120 ms

Broad monomorphic R in I, V5, V6 (often notched) 
Deep S or QS pattern in V1 
ST and T wave changes are expected (discordant to QRS);   new LBBB in the setting of
chest pain is a STEMI equivalent   — consider Sgarbossa criteria for ischemia in LBBB 
Fascicular Blocks (Hemiblocks) 
Left Anterior Fascicular Block (LAFB): 
Left axis deviation (−45° to −90°) 
Small Q in I and aVL, small R in II, III, aVF 
QRS < 120 ms 
Left Posterior Fascicular Block (LPFB): 
Right axis deviation (+90° to +180°) 
Small R in I and aVL, small Q in II, III, aVF 
QRS < 120 ms 
Much rarer; diagnose only after excluding RVH, lateral MI 
Bifascicular block:   RBBB + LAFB or RBBB + LPFB.   Trifascicular block:   Bifascicular block + 
fi rst-degree AV block (historical term; imprecise but still used). 
9. Chamber Enlargement and Hypertrophy 
Left Atrial Enlargement (LAE) 
Lead II: P wave > 120 ms, notched ("P mitrale") 
V1: terminal negative de fl ection ≥ 1 mm deep and ≥ 40 ms wide 
Right Atrial Enlargement (RAE) 
Lead II: P wave ≥ 2.5 mm tall ("P pulmonale") 
V1: initial positive de fl ection ≥ 1.5 mm 
Left Ventricular Hypertrophy (LVH) 
Sokolow-Lyon:   S in V1 + R in V5 or V6 ≥ 35 mm   Cornell voltage:   R in aVL + S in V3 > 28 mm
(men) or > 20 mm (women)   Romhilt-Estes point score:   more speci fi c, uses multiple criteria

Associated   fi ndings: LAE, left axis deviation, repolarization abnormalities (LV "strain" —
downsloping ST depression and T-wave inversion in lateral leads). 
Right Ventricular Hypertrophy (RVH) 
Right axis deviation 
R/S ratio > 1 in V1 
Deep S waves in V5, V6 
Right atrial enlargement often coexists 
RV "strain": T-wave inversion in V1–V3 
10. Ischemia and Infarction 
Recognizing STEMI 
Criteria (new guidelines):   ST elevation at the J point in two contiguous leads: 
≥ 1 mm in most leads 
≥ 2 mm (men) or ≥ 1.5 mm (women) in V2–V3 
≥ 0.5 mm in V7–V9 (posterior) or V3R–V4R (right-sided) 
Localization of Infarction 
Location   ST Elevation   Reciprocal ST
Depression 
Likely   Artery 
Anterior   V1–V4   II, III, aVF   LAD 
Anteroseptal   V1–V2   —   LAD
(proximal) 
Lateral   I, aVL, V5, V6   II, III, aVF   LCx or
diagonal 
Inferior   II, III, aVF   I, aVL   RCA (or LCx) 
Posterior   V7–V9 (reciprocal ST depression in V1–V3
with tall R) 
V1–V3   RCA or LCx 
Right
ventricular 
V3R, V4R   —   Proximal RCA

Always Get Right-Sided and Posterior Leads for Inferior MI 
Up to 40% of inferior MIs have RV involvement. Missing this is clinically important: nitrates can
cause severe hypotension in RV infarct; treatment is   fl uids. 
Non-STEMI / Ischemic Patterns 
ST depression   (horizontal or downsloping, ≥ 0.5 mm): subendocardial ischemia 
T-wave inversion   (symmetric, deep): ischemia or post-ischemic 
Dynamic changes   on serial EKGs carry more weight than a single tracing 
Q Waves 
Pathologic Q waves: ≥ 40 ms wide OR > 25% of R-wave height in that lead. Suggest completed
(old or evolving) infarction. Exception: Q in aVR and isolated small Q in V1 can be normal. 
High-Risk Patterns You Must Recognize 
Wellens Syndrome:   Deep symmetric T-wave inversions (Type B) or biphasic T waves (Type A)
in V2–V3, typically in a pain-free patient. Indicates a critical proximal LAD stenosis. Needs cath,
not stress testing. 
De Winter T Waves:   Upsloping ST depression at the J point in precordial leads with tall,
symmetric T waves. STEMI equivalent — proximal LAD occlusion. 
Sgarbossa Criteria (for MI in LBBB or paced rhythm): 
Concordant ST elevation ≥ 1 mm: 5 points 
Concordant ST depression ≥ 1 mm in V1–V3: 3 points 
Discordant ST elevation ≥ 5 mm: 2 points 
Score ≥ 3 is speci fi c for MI. The   modi fi ed Smith-Sgarbossa   replaces the last criterion with
a ratio of ST elevation to S-wave depth ≤ −0.25 and is more sensitive. 
aVR ST elevation > 1 mm   with di ff use ST depression suggests left main disease, triple-vessel
disease, or di ff use subendocardial ischemia. 
11. Electrolyte Abnormalities 
Potassium 
Hyperkalemia (progressive changes): 
1.   Peaked, narrow-based T waves (early; K ~5.5–6.5)

2.   P wave   fl attening and PR prolongation 
3.   QRS widening 
4.   Merging of QRS with T → "sine wave" (imminent arrest) 
5.   Asystole or VF 
Hypokalemia: 
Flattened T waves 
ST depression 
Prominent U waves 
Prolonged QT (actually QU) 
Predisposes to torsades 
Calcium 
Hypercalcemia:   Short QT, short ST segment, Osborn J waves in severe cases 
Hypocalcemia:   Prolonged QT (prolonged ST segment speci fi cally) 
Magnesium 
Hypomagnesemia:   Often mirrors hypokalemia; promotes torsades 
Hypermagnesemia:   Bradycardia, PR/QRS prolongation, AV block 
12. Important "Can't-Miss" Patterns 
Wol ff -Parkinson-White (WPW) 
Short PR (< 120 ms) 
Delta wave (slurred upstroke of QRS) 
Wide QRS 
Secondary ST-T changes 
Risk: rapid atrial   fi brillation with conduction down the accessory pathway → VF. Avoid AV-
nodal blockers (adenosine, beta blockers, verapamil, digoxin) in AF with WPW. 
Brugada Syndrome 
Type 1: Coved ST elevation ≥ 2 mm in V1–V2 with T-wave inversion

Type 2: Saddleback ST elevation 
Associated with sudden cardiac death; genetic sodium channel disorder (SCN5A) 
Long QT Syndromes 
Congenital or acquired. QTc > 500 ms is the danger zone. Seek and correct electrolytes and QT-
prolonging medications. 
Pericarditis 
Di ff use concave-up   ST elevation (not con fi ned to a vascular territory) 
PR depression   (especially in II; PR elevation in aVR) 
Typically no reciprocal ST depression (except aVR/V1) 
Evolves through four Spodick stages 
Pulmonary Embolism 
Sinus tachycardia is the most common   fi nding 
S1Q3T3   pattern (deep S in I, Q and inverted T in III) — classic but uncommon 
Right axis deviation, new incomplete RBBB 
T-wave inversions in V1–V4 (right heart strain) 
Digoxin E ff ect vs. Toxicity 
E ff ect:   "Scooped" / "Salvador Dalí mustache" ST depression, short QT 
Toxicity:   Virtually any arrhythmia, but classic   fi ndings include atrial tachycardia with
block, bidirectional VT, frequent PVCs 
Hypothermia 
Osborn (J) waves   — positive de fl ection at J point 
Bradycardia, prolonged intervals, muscle tremor artifact 
Early Repolarization 
Notched or slurred J point with concave ST elevation 
Usually in young, healthy patients 
Most common in precordial leads 
Diagnosis of exclusion

Takotsubo ("Stress") Cardiomyopathy 
Often mimics anterior STEMI 
Deep T-wave inversions and marked QT prolongation in evolving phase 
Clinical context matters: emotional stressor, post-menopausal woman, apical ballooning on
echo, clean coronaries on angiography 
13. Pacemakers 
Pacing Spikes 
Sharp vertical de fl ections immediately preceding the paced complex. Modern bipolar pacers
produce small spikes that can be subtle. 
Nomenclature (NASPE/BPEG Code) 
Five letters;   fi rst three are most used clinically: 
1.   Chamber paced (A, V, D = both, O = none) 
2.   Chamber sensed 
3.   Response to sensing (I = inhibited, T = triggered, D = both) 
Examples: 
VVI:   Ventricular pace, ventricular sense, inhibited by native beats 
DDD:   Dual-chamber pace and sense with both inhibition and triggering 
Troubleshooting 
Failure to capture:   Spike without following depolarization (lead dislodgement, battery
depletion, electrolytes) 
Failure to sense (undersensing):   Pacer   fi res despite native beats 
Oversensing:   Pacer inhibited when it shouldn't be (T-wave oversensing, myopotentials) 
Ischemia in a Paced Rhythm 
Use modi fi ed Sgarbossa criteria, as with LBBB.

Common artifacts that fool readers: 
Lead reversal   (LA/RA): inverted P and QRS in lead I — mimics dextrocardia 
Muscle tremor:   rapid irregular baseline (e.g., Parkinson's, shivering) — can mimic AF 
60-Hz interference:   regular   fi ne oscillation 
Wandering baseline:   respiration or loose electrode 
Lead disconnection:   fl at line in a single lead 
Always con fi rm dysrhythmias in more than one lead before acting. 
15. Quick Reference Summary 
Normal Values at a Glance 
Parameter   Normal Range 
Rate   60–100 bpm 
P wave   < 120 ms, < 2.5 mm 
PR interval   120–200 ms 
QRS   < 120 ms 
QTc   < 440 ms (M) / < 460 ms (W) 
R-wave progression   R > S by V3–V4 
Axis   −30° to +90° 
Always Ask Yourself 
1.   Is this rhythm stable? 
2.   Is this a STEMI or STEMI equivalent? 
3.   Is the QT dangerously long? 
4.   Is the QRS unexpectedly wide — and why? 
5.   Does the EKG match the clinical picture?

The Most Common Traps 
Assuming a wide-complex tachycardia is SVT with aberrancy — it's VT until proven
otherwise 
Missing posterior or right-sided MI because you only looked at the standard 12 leads 
Calling it sinus rhythm when the "P" is actually a retrograde or   fl utter wave 
Reading a half-standard or double-standard EKG at face value 
Treating the tracing without looking at the patient 
These notes are a study and clinical reference aid. Always correlate EKG   fi ndings with clinical
context, serial tracings, and appropriate advanced imaging or biomarker data. Do not use any
document as a substitute for formal training, supervised practice, or specialist consultation in real
patient care.
